theory.overview: Garbage Collection (GC) automatically reclaims memory that is no longer reachable by the program—eliminating manual memory management bugs like use-after-free and memory leaks. Languages like Java, JavaScript, Python, and Go use GC to provide memory safety. Understanding how GC works helps you write GC-friendly code, diagnose performance issues, and tune collection behavior. From simple reference counting to sophisticated generational collectors, GC algorithms represent a beautiful intersection of theory and practical engineering.

sections.title: Why Garbage Collection?
sections.content: Manual memory management is error-prone: forgetting to free causes leaks, freeing too early causes crashes, double-free corrupts memory. GC eliminates entire classes of bugs at the cost of some runtime overhead. Modern GCs are highly optimized—generational collection, concurrent marking, and incremental collection keep pause times minimal. For most applications, the productivity and safety gains outweigh the performance costs.
keyPoints: Eliminates memory leaks and dangling pointers
Runtime overhead is typically < 10% for modern GCs

sections.title: Reference Counting
sections.content: The simplest GC approach: each object tracks how many references point to it. When count reaches zero, the object is immediately freed. Pros: deterministic destruction, simple implementation, no pause times. Cons: circular references leak (A↔B never reaches zero), overhead on every pointer write, cache-unfriendly due to frequent count updates. Python and Swift use reference counting with cycle detection.
sections.diagram:
A → B → C (A.count=1, B.count=2, C.count=1)
When A freed: B.count=1
When nothing references B or C: they leak if B↔C cycle exists
keyPoints: Atomic operations needed for thread safety
Write barrier on every reference assignment

sections.title: Mark and Sweep
sections.content: The classic tracing GC algorithm with two phases. Mark: start from roots (global variables, stack, registers), traverse all reachable objects, mark them as alive. Sweep: scan entire heap, free unmarked objects. This handles cycles correctly (if not reachable from roots, collected). Downsides: pauses for entire heap traversal, fragmentation after many collections, memory not reclaimed until sweep.

phases.description: DFS/BFS from roots, set 'marked' flag on reachable objects
Scan heap, return unmarked objects to free list

sections.title: Generational Collection
sections.content: Based on the generational hypothesis: most objects die young. The heap is divided into generations: young (eden, survivor spaces) and old (tenured). New objects allocate in eden. Minor GC collects eden, promoting survivors to survivor spaces. Objects surviving multiple minor GCs promote to old gen. Major GC collects old gen, triggered less frequently. This makes common case (young object death) fast.

sections.title: Copying Collection
sections.content: Used in generational GC for young objects. Heap split into two semi-spaces: From and To. Allocate in From. When full, copy live objects to To, update references, swap spaces. Dead objects are left behind implicitly—no sweep phase needed. Pros: no fragmentation, allocation is fast (bump pointer), collection time proportional to live objects (not heap size). Cons: 2x memory overhead, long-lived objects copied repeatedly.
process: 2. When From full: trace from roots
3. Copy live objects to To space (compact)

sections.title: Concurrent and Incremental GC
sections.content: To reduce pause times, modern GCs work concurrently with the application. Challenge: the mutator (application) changes pointers while collector traces—can miss objects or trace garbage. Solution: write barriers log pointer changes, SATB (Snapshot-At-The-Beginning) or incremental update algorithms ensure correctness. Go's tri-color concurrent mark-sweep, Java's G1 and ZGC, .NET's concurrent GC all use these techniques to achieve sub-millisecond pauses.

techniques.name: Tri-color Marking
techniques.description: White (unvisited), Grey (reachable, children not scanned), Black (fully processed). Mutator write barriers maintain invariant.

techniques.name: SATB
techniques.description: Snapshot at start of mark: objects white→grey when overwritten pointer discovered

techniques.name: Incremental
techniques.description: Interleave small collection work between mutator execution

techniques.name: Concurrent
techniques.description: GC threads run parallel with mutator threads

keyConcepts.name: Root Set
keyConcepts.description: Starting points for tracing: global variables, CPU registers, stack frames. Anything directly accessible without following pointers.
keyConcepts.examples: Global variables, local variables on stack, static fields

keyConcepts.name: Reachability
keyConcepts.description: An object is reachable if there's a path from any root to it following references. Unreachable objects are garbage.

keyConcepts.name: Write Barrier
keyConcepts.description: Code executed when a pointer is written. Logs the change for the collector, maintains tri-color invariant, or updates remembered set.
keyConcepts.overhead: Small constant cost on every pointer store

keyConcepts.name: Promotion
keyConcepts.description: Moving objects from young generation to old generation after surviving multiple collections.

steps.title: Identify Root Set
steps.description: Scan global variables, stack frames, and registers to find all directly accessible objects. Mark these as reachable.

steps.title: Mark Phase - Trace References
steps.description: From each root, recursively follow all references. Mark every reachable object. Use DFS or BFS traversal.

steps.title: Mark Complete
steps.description: All reachable objects are marked. Unmarked objects are garbage (unreachable from any root).

steps.title: Sweep Phase (or Copy)
steps.description: Mark-Sweep: free unmarked objects. Copying: copy marked objects to new space, leave garbage behind.

steps.title: Compaction (Optional)
steps.description: Move live objects together to eliminate fragmentation. Update all references to new locations.

steps.title: Resume Application
steps.description: GC complete. Application threads resume. Freed memory available for new allocations.

practiceProblems.title: Reference Counting Basics
practiceProblems.description: Object A has count=2. One reference is set to null. What happens?
practiceProblems.answer: Count becomes 1. Object NOT freed because count != 0.
practiceProblems.explanation: Reference counting only frees when count reaches exactly 0. One reference remains.

practiceProblems.title: Circular Reference Leak
practiceProblems.description: A→B and B→A, no external refs. Both counts=1. Are they garbage collected?
practiceProblems.answer: Not with pure reference counting. Yes with tracing GC.
practiceProblems.explanation: Pure reference counting: neither count reaches 0 (cycle). Tracing GC: neither reachable from roots, so both collected.

practiceProblems.title: Mark Phase Count
practiceProblems.description: Heap has 1000 objects. Mark phase visits 300. How many will sweep free?
practiceProblems.explanation: Mark visits reachable objects. Unvisited (unmarked) objects are unreachable = garbage. 1000 - 300 = 700 freed.

practiceProblems.title: Generational Hypothesis
practiceProblems.description: What is the 'generational hypothesis' in garbage collection?
practiceProblems.explanation: Empirical observation: ~90% of objects die within a few MB of allocation or minor GC cycles. Optimizing for young object death makes GC efficient.
hints: Young objects tend to die quickly

practiceProblems.title: Copying Collector Space
practiceProblems.description: Copying collector with 4MB heap. How much memory available for allocation?
practiceProblems.explanation: Copying collectors split heap into two semi-spaces (From and To). Only From is used for allocation. 4MB / 2 = 2MB usable.

practiceProblems.title: GC Pause Time
practiceProblems.description: Why do simple mark-sweep collectors cause pauses?
practiceProblems.answer: Must stop all application threads during mark and sweep
practiceProblems.explanation: The collector needs a consistent view of the heap. If mutator changes pointers during mark, objects can be missed (live objects collected = crash).

practiceProblems.title: Write Barrier Purpose
practiceProblems.description: Why do concurrent GCs need write barriers?
practiceProblems.answer: To track pointer changes made by mutator while collector runs
practiceProblems.explanation: Without tracking, mutator could hide reachable objects from collector (store to field already scanned). Write barrier logs changes for re-scanning.

practiceProblems.title: Tri-color Invariant
practiceProblems.description: In tri-color marking, what invariant must be maintained?
practiceProblems.answer: No black object may hold a reference directly to a white object
practiceProblems.explanation: If black (done scanning) → white (unvisited), and white has no other path to roots, collector will miss it. Grey objects are the 'frontier'—being scanned but children not yet visited.

practiceProblems.title: GC Performance Trade-off
practiceProblems.description: Why is generational GC faster than collecting entire heap?
practiceProblems.answer: Minor GC only scans young generation (small, high mortality), major GC infrequent
practiceProblems.explanation: Young gen is small and most objects die there—collecting it is fast and frees lots of memory. Old gen collected rarely. Total GC work reduced.
hints: Young gen small and high death rate

practiceProblems.title: Memory Fragmentation
practiceProblems.description: What causes fragmentation and how does copying/compaction solve it?
practiceProblems.answer: Fragmentation: dead objects leave holes. Copying/compaction moves live objects together, leaving contiguous free space.
practiceProblems.explanation: After many allocations/frees, free memory becomes scattered holes. Large objects can't fit despite total free space being sufficient. Compaction creates one large free block.

minigame.title: Garbage Collector Guardian
minigame.description: Protect the heap from memory leaks! Trace references, identify garbage, and reclaim memory. Visualize how different GC algorithms work and compete for efficiency on the leaderboard.
instructions: Watch objects allocate on the heap
Trace from roots to mark live objects
Click garbage objects to reclaim them
Try different GC strategies for bonus challenges

levels.name: Generational Guardian
levels.goal: Perform 5 minor GCs and 1 major GC successfully

levels.name: Concurrent Master
levels.goal: Complete 10 GC cycles with <5ms max pause time

visualizer.title: Garbage Collection Visualizer
visualizer.description: Interactive visualization of GC algorithms. Watch mark-and-sweep, generational, and copying collectors in action. See the heap layout, reference graph, and collection phases step by step.

snippets.title: Simple Mark-and-Sweep GC
snippets.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import List, Optional, Set, Dict

@dataclass
class GCObject:
    id: int
    marked: bool = False
    refs: List['GCObject'] = field(default_factory=list)
    size: int = 1
    
    def __repr__(self):
        return f'Obj({self.id}, marked={self.marked}, refs={[r.id for r in self.refs]})'

class SimpleGC:
    def __init__(self, heap_size: int = 100):
        self.heap: List[GCObject] = []
        self.roots: Set[GCObject] = set()
        self.heap_size = heap_size
        self.next_id = 0
        self.freed_count = 0
    
    def allocate(self, size: int = 1) -> Optional[GCObject]:
        if len(self.heap) >= self.heap_size:
            print('Heap full, triggering GC...')
            self.collect()
            if len(self.heap) >= self.heap_size:
                return None  # Out of memory even after GC
        
        obj = GCObject(id=self.next_id, size=size)
        self.next_id += 1
        self.heap.append(obj)
        return obj
    
    def add_root(self, obj: GCObject):
        self.roots.add(obj)
    
    def remove_root(self, obj: GCObject):
        self.roots.discard(obj)
    
    def write_ref(self, from_obj: GCObject, to_obj: Optional[GCObject], idx: int = 0):
        '''Write barrier: update reference from from_obj to to_obj'''
        if idx < len(from_obj.refs):
            from_obj.refs[idx] = to_obj if to_obj else None
        elif to_obj:
            from_obj.refs.append(to_obj)
    
    def mark(self):
        '''Mark phase: trace from roots, mark reachable'''
        # Reset all marks
        for obj in self.heap:
            obj.marked = False
        
        # DFS from roots
        stack = list(self.roots)
        while stack:
            obj = stack.pop()
            if obj and not obj.marked:
                obj.marked = True
                for ref in obj.refs:
                    if ref and not ref.marked:
                        stack.append(ref)
    
    def sweep(self):
        '''Sweep phase: remove unmarked objects'''
        survivors = []
        freed = 0
        for obj in self.heap:
            if obj.marked:
                survivors.append(obj)
            else:
                freed += obj.size
                self.freed_count += 1
        
        self.heap = survivors
        return freed
    
    def collect(self) -> int:
        '''Full GC cycle: mark then sweep'''
        print(f'\n=== GC Start: {len(self.heap)} objects ===')
        
        # Mark phase
        self.mark()
        marked = sum(1 for obj in self.heap if obj.marked)
        print(f'Mark phase: {marked} objects reachable from roots')
        
        # Sweep phase
        freed = self.sweep()
        print(f'Sweep phase: {freed} bytes freed, {len(self.heap)} objects remain')
        
        print('=== GC Complete ===')
        return freed
    
    def heap_stats(self):
        total = sum(obj.size for obj in self.heap)
        marked = sum(1 for obj in self.heap if obj.marked)
        return {
            'objects': len(self.heap),
            'bytes_used': total,
            'bytes_free': self.heap_size - total,
            'reachable': marked
        }

# Demo
gc = SimpleGC(heap_size=20)

# Create objects
a = gc.allocate()
b = gc.allocate()
c = gc.allocate()
d = gc.allocate()

# Set up reference graph: a -> b -> c, and a -> d
gc.add_root(a)
gc.write_ref(a, b)
gc.write_ref(b, c)
gc.write_ref(a, d, idx=1)

# b is reachable from root a, but let's make it unreachable
gc.write_ref(a, None)  # Remove a's ref to b
# Now only d is reachable from a (through a.refs[1])

print('Before GC:', gc.heap_stats())
for obj in gc.heap:
    print(f'  {obj}')

gc.collect()

print('\nAfter GC:', gc.heap_stats())
for obj in gc.heap:
    print(f'  {obj}')

# Create a circular reference: x <-> y
x = gc.allocate()
y = gc.allocate()
gc.write_ref(x, y)
gc.write_ref(y, x)
# Neither is a root - they should be collected despite the cycle

print('\nAdded circular reference (no roots):')
gc.collect()
print('Circular objects collected:', gc.freed_count, 'total freed')
